source: Soll, Milkman, Payne (2015) A User's Guide to Debiasing (Wiley Blackwell Handbook of JDM, ch. 33)
finding: Frames debiasing as two families: modify the person (education, strategies, thinking rules) or modify the environment (defaults, incentives, accountability, choice architecture, checklists, models). A fix must match the bias source: a System 1 error, a missing normative rule, or low decision readiness.
numbers: No single effect size. Six criteria for choosing a method: effectiveness, decision readiness, competence/benevolence, heterogeneity, decision frequency, decision complexity.
limits: Review, not an experiment. Authors say more research is needed and urge testing each method in its own context.
agent_relevance: Matches our schema split: the program (environment) does the checking and the model only fills slots. Debiasing should match the error type, not be a blanket reminder.

source: Soll, Milkman, Payne (2015) A User's Guide to Debiasing (Wiley Blackwell Handbook of JDM, ch. 33)
finding: A System 2 correction needs three things: attention, knowledge of the right normative rule, and the skill to apply it. System 2 cannot help if the rule is unknown.
numbers: Example given: Bayes rule is needed to temper optimism about a garage startup (low base rate, WYSIATI).
limits: Conceptual claim; the dual-system split is itself criticised (Keren and Schul 2009, cited there).
agent_relevance: Telling the model to think carefully is not enough. The scaffold must supply the rule (base rate, reference class) and code must apply it.

source: Soll, Milkman, Payne (2015) A User's Guide to Debiasing (Wiley Blackwell Handbook of JDM, ch. 33)
finding: Statistical training transfers to new domains in the lab, but the transfer fades over weeks. Economics professors apply sunk-cost logic more than humanities or biology professors.
numbers: Cites Fong and Nisbett 1991 (delayed transfer, fades over weeks) and Larrick, Morgan, Nisbett 1990 (economists ignore sunk costs more).
limits: Second-hand report of the founding Nisbett-school studies; exact numbers are not in this chapter.
agent_relevance: Rules learned in one context do not generalise by themselves. A scaffold should re-inject the rule at the point of use, not rely on prior training.

source: Soll, Milkman, Payne (2015) A User's Guide to Debiasing (Wiley Blackwell Handbook of JDM, ch. 33)
finding: Consider-the-opposite (give reasons your first answer may be wrong) and prospective hindsight (imagine the project already failed, explain why) are offered to temper optimism. Authors say prospective hindsight might be even better but evidence is thin.
numbers: Prospective hindsight rests on Mitchell, Russo, Pennington 1989 (people find more causal paths for a past failure than a future one). No field effect size is given for either technique.
limits: Consider-the-opposite can backfire in hindsight tasks (see Lilienfeld 2009 lines).
agent_relevance: A pre-mortem step is a candidate operator but must fire on a signal (G1), not on a schedule. Our own data show forced doubt lowered accuracy (92% to 75%).

source: Soll, Milkman, Payne (2015) A User's Guide to Debiasing (Wiley Blackwell Handbook of JDM, ch. 33)
finding: Interval overconfidence is cut by splitting the question: ask for the 10th, 50th and 90th percentile instead of one range. Hit rate rises about 20 percentage points because intervals get wider and better centred. Bins (SPIES) work the same way.
numbers: Soll and Klayman 2004: about +20 points hit rate. CFOs' 80% intervals for S&P returns held the truth only 33% of the time (Ben-David, Graham, Harvey 2013).
limits: Reduces but does not erase overprecision. The 20-point figure is as stated by the chapter, not re-derived from the original.
agent_relevance: Sampling a distribution in bins or fractiles and reading it with code is a calibration tool we can copy for LLM numeric estimates.

source: Soll, Milkman, Payne (2015) A User's Guide to Debiasing (Wiley Blackwell Handbook of JDM, ch. 33)
finding: The crowd within: averaging a person's two answers to the same question gives about half of the accuracy gain of averaging two different people. A time delay between answers helps.
numbers: Larrick, Mannes, Soll 2012: within-person average gives about half of the between-person gain. Vul and Pashler 2008: delay helps.
limits: Gain exists only when the two answers bracket the truth. Answers from one mind share errors.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G4: repeated samples from one model are partly correlated, so averaging them captures at best a fraction of the crowd benefit.

source: Soll, Milkman, Payne (2015) A User's Guide to Debiasing (Wiley Blackwell Handbook of JDM, ch. 33)
finding: Money and accountability help only when the bias comes from low effort. Otherwise people think harder but not smarter and may do worse. Incentivised people tried to improve a reliable formula with idiosyncratic knowledge and did worse.
numbers: Arkes, Dawes, Christensen 1986 (cited): rewarded people did worse than unrewarded ones against the formula. Accountability helps sunk-cost avoidance (Simonson and Nye 1992).
limits: Mixed literature (Camerer and Hogarth 1999). Effect depends on whether the person knows the right rule.
agent_relevance: More compute or try-harder prompts will not fix a wrong model of the task. Spend budget on independent checks, not longer reasoning by the same model.

source: Soll, Milkman, Payne (2015) A User's Guide to Debiasing (Wiley Blackwell Handbook of JDM, ch. 33)
finding: Checklists reduce errors from forgetting and availability and are most useful in complex, stressful, repeated tasks. Linear models, checklists and fixed policies can sharply improve accuracy in repeated decisions such as admissions or diagnosis.
numbers: Hales and Pronovost 2006 and Gawande 2010 cited, no number given. Planning prompt for colonoscopy: 85% screened vs 63% with an opt-out default (Narula et al. 2013). Default enrolment can add 37 points (Madrian and Shea 2001).
limits: Checklists help execution of known steps. They do not by themselves fix judgement biases like anchoring.
agent_relevance: Supports code-enforced step lists, but see schema 4b: a checklist the model reads and self-reports on is not a check.

source: Lilienfeld, Ammirati, Landfield (2009) Giving debiasing away
finding: Debiasing research is far smaller than bias cataloguing. Evidence on debiasing confirmation bias is thin, lacks a unifying theory and is mixed. Consider-the-opposite and consider-an-alternative help at least somewhat; delayed decision helped clinicians.
numbers: PsycInfo search of 19 June 2008: 1,211 hits for cognitive bias(es) vs 158 for debias(ing). Cites Lord, Lepper, Preston 1984; Hirt and Markman 1995; Koriat, Lichtenstein, Fischhoff 1980; Spengler et al. 1995 (delay).
limits: Narrative review focused on confirmation bias; no pooled effect size.
agent_relevance: Confirms the asymmetry: finding bias is easy, removing it is hard. Treat each debiasing step as untested until measured on our tasks.

source: Lilienfeld, Ammirati, Landfield (2009) Giving debiasing away
finding: Teaching about biases alone is disputed. Arkes (1981) called psychoeducation by itself absolutely worthless. Others find it works in some studies. The most successful critical-thinking programs teach metacognitive rules such as consider alternative points of view.
numbers: Cites Willingham 2007 (critical-thinking programs at best modestly effective) and Lehman and Nisbett 1990 (rule training).
limits: The Arkes quote is as reported by Lilienfeld, not read at source.
agent_relevance: Awareness prompts (beware of anchoring) are the LLM version of psychoeducation. Expect little gain unless tied to a rule and a check.

source: Lilienfeld, Ammirati, Landfield (2009) Giving debiasing away
finding: Debiasing can backfire. Asking people to list many alternative outcomes raised their certainty that the original outcome was inevitable, because listing many was hard (availability). The bias blind spot also makes people see debiasing as meant for others.
numbers: Sanna, Schwarz, Stocker 2002 (hindsight backfire). Pronin et al. 2004 (bias blind spot).
limits: Backfire shown for hindsight bias; whether it happens for consider-the-opposite on confirmation bias is stated as unclear.
agent_relevance: Forced list-alternatives steps can raise confidence in the wrong answer. Fits our measured finding that forced doubt hurt.

source: Morewedge et al. (2015) Debiasing decisions: improved decision making with a single training intervention
finding: Experiment 1: one 30-minute session (a serious game with feedback, or an instructional video) cut bias blind spot, confirmation bias and fundamental attribution error. The game beat the video and gains lasted two months.
numbers: N=278 recruited; 243 completed lab (Game 160, Video 83); 196 follow-up (Game 130, Video 66). Mean bias reduction: game -46.25% immediately and -34.76% at 2 months; video -18.60% and -20.10%.
limits: Convenience sample in Pittsburgh. Bias scales are built by the authors with items close to the training items. Not a field outcome.
agent_relevance: Feedback plus practice on cases beats exposition. For an agent, feedback-driven correction on worked examples beats a one-line warning.

source: Morewedge et al. (2015) Debiasing decisions: improved decision making with a single training intervention
finding: Experiment 2: game and video also reduced anchoring, projection and representativeness, with persistence at about three months. Game larger than video again.
numbers: N=269 recruited; 238 completed lab (Game 156, Video 82); 192 follow-up (Game 126, Video 66). Game -31.94% immediately, -23.57% at 3 months; video -25.70% and -19.20%.
limits: Same lab-only limits. Follow-up attrition about 20 percent.
agent_relevance: Effects shrink with time (46 to 35 points, 32 to 24) but stay positive. A stateless LLM has no persistence, so correction must be re-applied every run.

source: Morewedge et al. (2015) Debiasing decisions: improved decision making with a single training intervention
finding: Training transferred to untrained facets of confirmation bias. Gains on untrained facets were about as large as on trained ones and equal at follow-up.
numbers: Trained facets d=0.78 (posttest) and d=0.24 (follow-up); untrained facets d=0.79 and d=0.65. Trained vs untrained facets at posttest d=0.20; no difference at follow-up.
limits: Pre-post within-subject design; the only comparison arm is the video.
agent_relevance: Some transfer across items of the same bias is plausible when training teaches the general rule. Supports rule-level scaffolds over item-level patches.

source: Sellier, Scopelliti, Morewedge (2019) Debiasing training improves decision making in the field
finding: Field test: MBA and master students played a confirmation-bias game, and chance timing meant some played before an unannounced Challenger-style launch case. Trained students were less likely to choose the inferior hypothesis-confirming option.
numbers: N=290 (trained 182, untrained 108). Chose to race: 58.8% trained vs 72.2% untrained; beta=-0.60, p=.022, odds ratio 0.549 (95% CI .33 to .92). Case completion 73.1% vs 63.0%, ns (p=.071).
limits: Single field experiment; quasi-random assignment through the training schedule; graduate business students. Effect larger in narrow day windows (48.0% vs 72.7% within a 4-day window).
agent_relevance: Best human evidence that a short bias-specific intervention changes a later, different decision. Still needs an independent replication.

source: Sellier, Scopelliti, Morewedge (2019) Debiasing training improves decision making in the field
finding: The training effect did not fade between 1 and 52 days before the case. Coded case write-ups point to less confirmatory hypothesis testing as the mechanism.
numbers: Short-lag group 56.8% vs long-lag 63.2% choosing to race, difference ns (p=.419). Trained students wrote fewer confirming statements (M 1.45 vs 2.07, d=.39); the gap for disconfirming statements was ns (d=.11).
limits: Mechanism inferred from coded write-ups, not manipulated.
agent_relevance: Supports judging debiasing by the process trace (what evidence was sought) as well as by the final answer. Code can count disconfirming tests actually run.

source: Haran, Moore, Morewedge (2010) A simple remedy for overprecision in judgment (SPIES)
finding: SPIES: give judges the whole outcome range cut into bins and ask for each bin's probability. Overprecision at the 90% level disappeared, while ordinary 90% intervals and fractile pairs stayed overprecise.
numbers: Exp 1 (N about 103; monthly Pittsburgh temperature): hit rate 88.35% for 90% SPIES vs 73.79% for 90% confidence intervals and 73.79% for 5th/95th fractiles; overprecision 16.21 points for the latter two (d=0.74); SPIES not different from 90% (p=.60). SPIES wider (31.81 vs 23.58, d=0.62).
limits: Three experiments, online convenience samples, numeric estimation. Midpoint accuracy was no better, so the gain is wider intervals, not more knowledge.
agent_relevance: A forced full-distribution format is a structural fix. For LLM numeric answers, ask for bin probabilities and let code derive the interval.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: BiasBuster dataset of 13,465 prompts tests anchoring (sequential), status quo, primacy, framing and group attribution in college-admission decisions on GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Llama-2 7B/13B. Models show bias-like patterns that differ by model.
numbers: GPT-4 admits 40.5% more students under the reject framing (Table 3 baseline: admit 0.375 vs reject 0.780, gap -0.405). Llama-2 7B classifies 32.1% fewer females as good at math. No clear status-quo effect; for most models the status-quo option was chosen less.
limits: Synthetic admissions task. Llama-2 baseline rows hit near-zero admission rates (instruction failure), so some biased baselines are uninformative.
agent_relevance: Framing sensitivity is large even in a strong model. Our agent should state each decision in one neutral form and test both polarities in code.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: Prompt-based debiasing (awareness, contrastive and counterfactual few-shot examples) often broke instruction following. Few-shot debiasing drove admission or rejection rates to near 0 or 1. Zero-shot awareness gave small gains at best.
numbers: Table 3 flags instruction failures (<1% admit or reject). Llama-2 7B contrastive: admit 0.996, reject 1.000 (collapse). GPT-3.5 awareness framing gap 0.035 vs biased baseline 0.165; GPT-4 awareness gap -0.470 vs baseline -0.405 (no gain).
limits: Few-shot examples were hand-written per bias and changed the prompt a lot, which confounds the test.
agent_relevance: Supports schema 4b: static example lists and reminders are fragile and bias-specific. Keep any example step small and test for collapse.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: Self-help debiasing: the model rewrites the biased prompt itself and then answers the rewrite. It works best in the strongest model. Weak models change too many decisions.
numbers: GPT-4 framing gap -0.405 to -0.010; GPT-3.5 0.165 to -0.080 (sign flips). GPT-3.5 group-attribution gap got larger (0.085 to 0.150). In GPT-4 self-help left 0% biased group-attribution prompt elements and 2.7% biased framing elements. Llama models changed 40 to 52% of anchoring decisions when allowed to revise.
limits: Success needs a high-capacity model; the rewrite step can itself drift. Single synthetic domain.
agent_relevance: A normalise-the-prompt operator (strip framing, sources, defaults) is a cheap, code-checkable step. Check by answering both the original and the rewrite and comparing in code.

source: Lyu et al. (2025) Self-Adaptive Cognitive Debiasing for LLMs in Decision-Making (SACD)
finding: SACD iterates three steps (bias determination, bias analysis, debiasing rewrite) until no bias is found. On finance (FOMC), medical (PubMedQA) and legal (LegalBench) tasks it gives the lowest bias scores in single-bias and multi-bias prompts across four LLMs.
numbers: FOMC, llama3.1-8b average bias: vanilla 0.3805, CoT 0.3425, self-help 0.2100, SACD 0.1570. Across four models SACD averages 0.0300-0.1570 on FOMC, 0.0425-0.1790 on PubMedQA, 0.0400-0.1235 on LegalBench vs best baselines 0.0625-0.3490, 0.0725-0.4175, 0.0725-0.2625.
limits: Bias score is an answer shift under injected bias text (anchor, bandwagon, loss aversion), not accuracy on real decisions. Authors designed the method.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM analogue to a signal-triggered loop: rewrite only while a detector fires. Our code can compare answers with and without the injected cue.

source: Lyu et al. (2025) Self-Adaptive Cognitive Debiasing for LLMs in Decision-Making (SACD)
finding: Baselines that sound like good practice did not remove bias. Chain of thought gave modest gains. Reflexion and multi-agent debate raised bias in multi-bias settings. Few-shot debiasing often made things worse.
numbers: FOMC llama3.1-8b average bias: multi-agent debate 0.5020, few-shot 0.4215, few-shot debiasing 0.2970 (vanilla 0.3805). llama3.1-70b: vanilla 0.1648, few-shot 0.3655, few-shot debiasing 0.2900. gpt-3.5 multi-agent debate 0.5155 on FOMC. CoT range 0.2470-0.6150 across domains.
limits: Same bias-score metric; stronger models start lower, so gains differ by model size.
agent_relevance: Debate and self-reflection amplify a shared bias because agents echo each other. Matches G4: no same-model voters or debate to remove a shared bias.

source: Lyu et al. (2025) Self-Adaptive Cognitive Debiasing for LLMs in Decision-Making (SACD)
finding: Error analysis with gpt-3.5: self-help debiasing mostly detects bias but does not remove it (insufficient debiasing). SACD removes that error type but adds bias misjudgement and bias confusion.
numbers: Total errors out of 500: finance self-help 257 (51.4%) vs SACD 61 (12.2%); medical 209 (41.8%) vs 111 (22.2%); legal 409 (81.8%) vs 79 (15.8%). SACD errors were mostly bias confusion (49, 108, 73) and misjudgement (12, 3, 6).
limits: Model-judged bias labels. Version read is a long preprint (v4, Nov 2025), not confirmed as peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: Detect-then-fix by the same model fails at the fix step. Having code do the fix (swap, neutralise) avoids the knows-but-cannot-remove gap.

source: Itzhak et al. (2024) Instructed to Bias: instruction-tuned LMs exhibit emergent cognitive bias
finding: Instruction tuning and RLHF increase decoy, certainty and belief-bias effects. Instruction-tuned models (Flan-T5, Mistral-Instruct, GPT-3.5, GPT-4) show stronger bias than base models. Larger Flan-T5 shows more bias on three of five scores.
numbers: GPT-4 accuracy 84% on belief tasks with bias scores 0.07 (belief valid) and 0.49 (belief invalid); decoy bias highest in GPT-4 among the GPT series. Flan-T5-XXL decoy-expensive score -0.18 (it chose the expensive option almost always in control). Belief-bias accuracy drop of 19% to 61% in treatment vs control.
limits: Cannot separate instruction tuning from RLHF for closed models; training data unknown. Bias score definitions differ per task.
agent_relevance: Alignment tuning is not debiasing. Do not assume a stronger or RLHF model is less biased; measure each cue on our model.

source: Lou and Sun (2024) Anchoring Bias in Large Language Models: An Experimental Study
finding: 62 anchoring questions (daily-life estimates with low, high and expert anchor hints). GPT-4, GPT-4o and GPT-3.5 are pulled by anchors. Chain of thought, thoughts of principles, ignore-the-hint and reflection do not remove it. Giving both a low and a high anchor brings answers near the no-anchor value on some items.
numbers: Dataset: 62 samples, 8 with an irrelevant H1 hint. Stronger models were more consistently anchored (9 of 11 non-significant exceptions came from GPT-3.5). 7 time-period questions gave 6 of 11 exceptions.
quote: simple algorithms such as Chain-of-Thought, Thoughts of Principles, Ignoring Anchor Hints, and Reflection are not sufficient
limits: Small question set, numeric answers, preprint by high-school authors. The both-anchor fix works on some items, not all.
agent_relevance: Supports collecting cues from several directions: give the model two opposed cues or none, rather than telling it to ignore one.

source: Suri et al. (2023) Do LLMs show decision heuristics similar to humans? (GPT-3.5)
finding: GPT-3.5 shows anchoring, conjunction-style likelihood errors, framing and endowment effects in four studies, matching human participants on the same prompts. Asked beforehand, it said it would not show such biases.
numbers: Anchoring (random 10-20 vs 100-200 anchor): GPT-3.5 mean estimates 20.83 (low) vs 105.97 (high), t(58)=8.78, p<.0001; humans 22.50 vs 80.50. GPT-4, 5 trials per condition: 22.0 vs 94.33.
limits: Small cells (about 30 per group), GPT-3.5 era, prompts rewritten for chat format.
agent_relevance: The model's own claim that it is unbiased is not evidence. The scaffold should not ask the model whether it is biased.

source: Jones and Steinhardt (2022) Capturing failures of LLMs via human cognitive biases
finding: In Codex and CodeGen, framing, anchoring and availability-like effects appear in code generation. Irrelevant preceding functions lower accuracy and models copy framing lines.
numbers: Irrelevant preceding functions cut functional accuracy by 22.3 to 30.5 points for Codex; framing line reproduced 81% (Codex) and 70.7% (CodeGen) vs 4.5% and 0.0% without. Operation-order flip: accuracy 50% to 17%. Attribute substitution: accuracy 100% to 4.4-4.6%.
limits: 2022 models. The paper maps biases to failures but does not test fixes.
agent_relevance: Prompt cues leak into outputs. Argues for test-by-perturbation (add and remove the cue) as a code check.

source: Malberg et al. (2024) A Comprehensive Evaluation of Cognitive Biases in LLMs
finding: A 30,000-test benchmark finds all 30 tested cognitive biases in at least some of 20 LLMs, with large differences between models. Tests are generated by template, not by hand.
numbers: 20 models, 30 biases, 30,000 tests. In one case a model could not decide in 33% of tests.
limits: Detection benchmark; the paper does not study debiasing. Only the abstract and introduction were read closely.
agent_relevance: A bias battery with perturbation tests could serve as a regression test of our scaffold (does a step shrink the framing gap).

source: Mellers et al. (2015) The psychology of intelligence analysis: drivers of prediction accuracy
finding: In the IARPA forecasting tournament (199 questions over 2 years) probabilistic-reasoning training and teamwork were both situational drivers of accuracy. Best forecasters combined good traits with training and teams, and did deliberate practice with frequent belief updating.
numbers: Multiple correlation .64 between a model with dispositions, training, teams and behaviour and Brier-based accuracy. Training was randomly assigned in Year 2.
limits: This paper reports the combined model, not a clean effect size for training alone (that is in Mellers et al. 2014, not opened).
agent_relevance: Reference-class and averaging training helped in a real, scored setting, so debiasing can survive outside the lab.

source: Fischhoff (1982) Debiasing (in Kahneman, Slovic, Tversky eds., Judgment under Uncertainty)
finding: Founding debiasing taxonomy: bias can come from the task, the judge, or the mismatch between them, and remedies fix one of those. Later authors call the early record a rocky start.
numbers: Not opened. Morewedge et al. 2015 describe a rocky start. No numbers recorded.
limits: Not read at source; chapter is paywalled.
agent_relevance: Source of the task-vs-person split used above.

source: Arkes (1991) Costs and benefits of judgment errors: implications for debiasing
finding: Tripartite taxonomy (strategy-based, association-based, psychophysical errors); each needs a different fix. Argues debiasing must be matched to error type, with accountability helping effort-limited errors.
numbers: Not opened; known only through citations in Lilienfeld 2009 and Soll et al. 2015.
limits: Taxonomy described second-hand.
agent_relevance: Supports matching the correction to the error class instead of one generic debiasing prompt.

source: Larrick (2004) Debiasing (Blackwell Handbook of JDM, pp. 316-337)
finding: Cited for three strategy families: motivational, cognitive (consider the opposite, rule training) and technological (linear models, group aggregation), and for the warning that more effort does not fix strategy-based errors.
numbers: Not opened; summary from Soll et al. 2015 and Lilienfeld 2009 citations.
limits: No PDF found this session.
agent_relevance: The technological family (models, aggregation) is the nearest human analogue of our code-run checks.

source: Lord, Lepper, Preston (1984) Considering the opposite: a corrective strategy for social judgment
finding: Founding consider-the-opposite study. Cited by Lilienfeld 2009 as showing that instructing people to consider the opposite reduces biased assimilation of evidence.
numbers: Not opened; effect sizes not recorded.
limits: Whether a plain be-unbiased instruction failed in the same study is from memory and not verified this session.
agent_relevance: If so, it matches the LLM finding that bare awareness prompts do little while a concrete opposite-case task works better.
